state: Sixteen existing registered local-draft owners selected at an audit-only source checkpoint. Selection is neither new authorship nor wholesale verification. No canonical field/id/date/link/alias/relation/registration changed. Prior full gates reused only by exact code/data and all graph fingerprints.

records.name: Synthetic cytokine receptors
records.tldr: An engineered cytokine receptor connects a specified input to signalling inside a cell. The added signal and the behaviour of the complete cell product need separate measurements.
records.summary: A synthetic cytokine receptor is an engineered cell-surface protein that connects a specified input to intracellular signalling. It differs from engineering a soluble cytokine or simply administering a cytokine. Some designs require an externally supplied ligand; others generate ligand-independent signalling. The receptor domains, input, expression and cell type define the tested construct. A growth-supporting signal does not itself establish antigen recognition, entry into a tumour, completed killing or durable patient benefit.

Wilkie 2010: IL-4-driven expansion and separate CAR targeting in human-cell experiments
Lunger 2026 macrophage receptor preprint; not a clinical report
Enoda: MIMIC platform description; sponsor naming and claims
Wu et al.: small-molecule ON-switch CAR experiments (2015)
FDA: Considerations for the Development of CAR T Cell Products (January 2024)

notes: Engelowski and colleagues joined fluorescent-protein-binding nanobodies to selected cytokine-receptor membrane and intracellular domains. Artificial GFP/mCherry-based ligands induced signalling in experimental systems. That 2018 study is a particular ligand-dependent design, not a test of every synthetic receptor or of a company platform with a different architecture.

In a 2010 human T-cell study, a chimeric receptor joined the IL-4 receptor binding region to an IL-2/IL-15 receptor signalling component. IL-4 supported expansion of the engineered cells, while a separate CAR specified the tumour target. The reported culture experiments distinguished expansion, cytokine dependence and target-cell killing; they were not patient efficacy results.

A 2026 macrophage preprint studied ligand-independent receptors with varied signalling motifs in primary human macrophages and preclinical models. Marker expression, phagocytosis and mouse tumour observations were different readouts. The report remains a preprint and does not establish human treatment benefit.

Enoda uses MIMIC as the name of its synthetic cytokine-receptor assets. The platform name does not define all engineered cytokine receptors or establish clinical performance. Its website describes platform aims and sponsor claims; it is not a comparative clinical safety or efficacy report.

For a drug-gated construct, withdrawing the input can reduce a selected signal without eliminating cells already engineered. Receptor signalling, viable-cell counts, tissue location, target-cell killing and later disease control need distinct measurements. A growth or activity switch is different from a cell-elimination mechanism.
A mechanistic schematic shows an intended arrangement. It is not a measurement of receptor expression, signalling, cell killing or patient outcome; each of those requires its own evidence.

In a fictional comparison with equal starting viable-cell input and the same CAR, a supplied trigger produces 250 viable cells at 48 hours versus 100 without it. That is 2.5 times the viable-cell count, not 2.5 times the treatment benefit. Tumour killing changes from 20 to 25 per cent, while a separate healthy-cell assay changes from two to 18 per cent injury. Count division, survival and loss separately, retain each assay’s target-cell denominator and uncertainty, and do not combine these results into a whole-body safety window.

Read each supportive feature as a testable hypothesis. A drug-triggered signal needs a baseline and a withdrawal test; an antigen-triggered signal needs testing after cells leave the priming site. Constitutive signalling raises different growth and cell-state questions, while a secreted payload can affect neighbouring cells or circulate. Orthogonal means sufficiently separate from natural partners under tested conditions, not selectivity established by its name. The supportive receptor does not specify the CAR target, and changing an internal signal is different from secreting a cytokine. An added support signal does not by itself demonstrate adequate oxygen, tissue access, recognition of an absent antigen or patient benefit.

records.name: Cytokine
records.tldr: Small proteins immune cells use to talk to each other: alarms, recruitment calls, growth orders and stand-down signals. Some are cancer drugs, and a flood of them is the danger of certain immunotherapies.
records.summary: Interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor and chemokines each act on cells carrying the matching receptor; IL-2 drives T-cell growth and was one of the first immunotherapies (aldesleukin), interferon-alpha was used in melanoma and leukaemia, and engineered cytokines aim to keep the benefit while losing the toxicity. Tumours secrete cytokines that recruit suppressive cells and drive inflammation, and IL-6 is a major driver of cancer cachexia. When CAR-T cells or T-cell engagers activate en masse they release cytokines in a surge (cytokine release syndrome), treated by blocking IL-6 with tocilizumab. A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response. A review of receptor biology said that all cytokines, to a greater or lesser extent, show pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions), and proposed that redundancy might be explained by related cytokines using a common receptor subunit, while pleiotropy requires that receptors exert different activities on different cells (Nicola, 1994). Different IL-2 and anti-IL-2 antibody complexes selectively expanded CD8 T cells or CD4 regulatory T cells in mice, so the formulation and the receiving cells mattered (Boyman et al., 2006). Chemokines help direct cell movement through gradients: in mouse skin an immobilised CCL21 gradient guided dendritic cells towards lymphatic vessels, and displacing or swamping it abolished directed migration (Weber et al., 2013), but movement also needs a compatible receptor and a traversable route. Measurements answer different questions: a concentration in picograms per millilitre of a named fluid, the percentage of a defined cell gate making a protein after stimulation, and RNA expression are different layers, a blood concentration does not reconstruct a tumour gradient, and two preparations can share an average (0 and 20, or 10 and 10, picograms per millilitre both average 10) while differing in spatial pattern. Intracellular cytokine staining usually involves a stimulation of a few hours (4 to 6 hours was usually sufficient to detect interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor), a block on secretion with brefeldin A or monensin so that the protein stays inside the cell, and negative and positive controls (Cossarizza et al., 2019). Calibration and a detection limit belong in the same report; that is OnCo's reporting advice and not a finding of the cited guideline. Chemokines are a family of cytokines and not a separate category, a growth-support signal such as IL-2 does not choose the antigen a T cell recognises, and more signal is not automatically more useful or safer immunity. For interferons, timing and the receiving cell mattered in mouse experiments: endogenous type I interferon was needed to prevent the growth of carcinogen-induced and transplanted tumours and acted through host blood-lineage cells (Dunn et al., 2005), whereas prolonged interferon signalling in experimental tumours maintained a resistance programme to checkpoint blockade (Benci et al., 2016). That a signal is tumour-associated does not by itself make it a safe target; this is OnCo's boundary statement and not a cited finding.

notes: Cytokines are signalling proteins whose binding to a suitable receptor changes signalling and gene expression in a receiving cell. Autocrine action is on the producing cell, paracrine action is on neighbours, and endocrine action is at a distance, for example after entry into the circulation. Distant action is possible rather than the default for every cytokine (British Society for Immunology, Cytokines: Introduction). Chemokines are a cytokine family involved in cell recruitment and can also affect leukocyte activation (NLM MeSH, Chemokines). The information-versus-fuel distinction is a reading rule: a measured amount of signalling protein does not measure the energy available to the cell, and a message without the relevant receptor and response machinery does not establish a response.

records.name: JAK-STAT signalling
records.tldr: The relay that turns cytokine signals into gene changes. Overactive in blood cancers (JAK2 in myelofibrosis), it is also the wire that carries interferon's cancer-killing message, so tumours cut it to escape immunotherapy.
records.summary: Cytokine receptors recruit JAK kinases that phosphorylate STAT transcription factors. JAK2 V617F drives myeloproliferative neoplasms (ruxolitinib, fedratinib, momelotinib approved); STAT3 is a hub for IL-6-driven survival, immunosuppression, and cachexia; STAT5 in leukaemias. Interferon-γ signalling via JAK1/2-STAT1 upregulates MHC and PD-L1; JAK1/2 loss-of-function mutations cause acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade. Direct STAT3 inhibitors (degraders, antisense) are in early trials.

links.label: Hu et al., The JAK/STAT signaling pathway: from bench to clinic (Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy 2021)
Synthetic cytokine receptors transmit biological signals using artificial ligands. (2018)
Inhibition of TGF-β-receptor signaling augments the antitumor function of ROR1-specific CAR T-cells against triple-negative breast cancer. (2020)

notes: Leading programmes: Levine (MSK) on JAK2 and MPN; Ribas (UCLA) on JAK mutations and PD-1 resistance; Darnell legacy (Rockefeller).

JAK-STAT is a route used by many cytokine receptors rather than a synonym for every cytokine response. Engelowski’s artificial receptor/ligand systems tested defined signalling and growth responses. Stüber’s TGF-beta experiments measured a SMAD-associated response in ROR1 CAR T cells. Follow the specified receptor and measured pathway through to gene output and cell phenotype; a phosphate signal, feedback response, growth measurement and completed target killing are different observations.
records.analogy: JAK-STAT is a doorbell wired to the house lights. Cytokines ring, JAK flips the switch, STAT turns on the lights. Cancers either jam the switch on (JAK2 mutation) or cut the wire so interferon cannot turn on the 'I am infected' lights.
interventions: JAK inhibitors in myeloproliferative neoplasms and GVHD
Anti-IL-6 (tocilizumab) for CRS and under study for cachexia
JAK-loss tumours: MHC-independent therapies (T-cell engagers, NK cells)

records.name: In vivo CAR-T
records.tldr: An in vivo delivery product carries receptor-encoding instructions into cells inside the body. Its dose is different from the later number and activity of engineered cells.
records.summary: Targeted delivery can supply CAR-encoding instructions to cells inside the body, using formats such as a viral vector or an mRNA lipid nanoparticle. This changes where engineering happens; it does not mean the active cells are donor-derived. Delivery targeting, cancer-antigen recognition, generated-cell abundance, receptor duration and useful function are separate questions. Conditioning, repeat dosing, safety and total cost belong to a specified product and protocol rather than to the in vivo label.

links.label: Pfeiffer et al., In vivo generation of human CD19-CAR T cells results in B-cell depletion and signs of cytokine release syndrome (EMBO Molecular Medicine 2018)
Rurik et al.: targeted mRNA nanoparticles in a mouse cardiac-injury model (2022)
ClinicalTrials.gov: INT2104 phase 1 oncology design, not an outcome report
FDA: CAR T-cell development guidance, January 2024
Hunter et al., 2025: human-cell, humanised-mouse and monkey experiments
In vivo generation of human CD19-CAR T cells results in B-cell depletion and signs of cytokine release syndrome. (2018)
A targeting lentiviral vector for generation of CAR-T cells in vivo. (2026)
Frank et al., 2020: CD3-targeted lentiviral delivery and humanised-mouse blood measurements

notes: Pfeiffer generated human CD19 CAR T cells with a CD8-targeted lentiviral vector in humanized mouse experiments. B-cell depletion and signs consistent with cytokine release syndrome were observed. This was a preclinical study, not a human clinical response report or evidence for freedom from inflammatory toxicity.

Rurik used targeted mRNA lipid nanoparticles to generate transient CAR T cells in a mouse cardiac-injury model. It demonstrates a delivery/expression approach in that setting; it does not establish cancer efficacy, human safety or an interchangeable regimen for other delivery formats.

The INT2104 registry NCT06539338 identifies a phase 1 B-cell-cancer study in the dated source check. A trial design or registry listing does not supply efficacy results, prove local slot availability or validate a platform-wide claim about conditioning.

A prepared carrier can engineer the recipient's own cells. Vector or nanoparticle dose, ongoing delivery, newly generated cells, cell proliferation and receptor persistence should be measured separately. Stopping carrier administration need not immediately end the activity of cells already engineered.

The cited preclinical results do not by themselves establish a fixed cost reduction, universal absence of lymphodepletion or automatic repeat-dose feasibility. Evaluate the actual process, monitoring and protocol rather than treating these as inherent benefits of all in vivo products.

Ex vivo describes engineering outside the body followed by administration of a cell product. In vivo engineering administers an instruction-carrying product and generates modified cells inside the body; it is not the same as testing an ex vivo product in an animal. Location, recipient versus donor origin and transient versus stable genetic fate are separate attributes.

In a fictional sampled population of 200 cells, 60 show the stated receptor measurement: 60/200 is 30% of that sampled population at that time. It does not specify a whole-body engineered-cell count, the administered carrier dose, tissue distribution, durable expression or killing. Sequence detection, expression, abundance and biological function need their own measurements.

Hunter's 2025 study used targeted mRNA nanoparticles in healthy-donor and autoimmune patient cell samples, humanised mice and cynomolgus monkeys. Tumour control in mice and B-cell depletion in monkeys are not human treatment outcomes. Quality testing of the administered carrier also cannot sample every subsequently engineered cell or tissue; relevant biodistribution, expression, kinetics and safety evidence is still needed.

Pfeiffer’s CD8-targeted lentiviral experiment used immunodeficient NSG mice engrafted with activated human blood mononuclear cells, with separate Raji-lymphoma conditions. Seven days after vector administration, CAR-positive cells represented 30 to 50 per cent of CD8-positive T cells in peritoneal fluid, 10 to 35 per cent in spleen and 5 to 30 per cent in blood; fewer than 0.5 per cent of CD8-negative T cells entered the CAR-positive gate. The appendix gates living cells through human CD45, then CD3 and CD8 before measuring CAR. Thus the CD8-negative comparison is within T cells, not every other cell in the body. Vehicle and reporter-vector controls, CD19-cell depletion and the starting target-cell population mattered. These later fractions combine delivery with survival and antigen-driven expansion; they are not pure entry efficiencies, whole-body exclusivity or human efficacy results.

A fictional 48-hour sample contains receptor expression in 60 of 200 viable T cells and five of 100 non-T cells. That is 30 per cent of T cells and five per cent of non-T cells; about 92 per cent of all expressing cells are T cells (60 of 65). None of these denominators establishes exclusive delivery. Compare matched carrier/receptor controls, antigen-positive and antigen-negative targets and relevant healthy cells. Sampling time, cell recovery and viable gates stay attached; a culture sample does not enumerate every tissue.

A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

Consider a complete fictional evidence packet, not a real therapy. Carrier P is a T-cell-directed lipid nanoparticle containing mRNA for CAR-X, which recognises extracellular epitope E on antigen X, and a separate supportive receptor R activated by trigger D. R does not add a cancer target, and P has no cell-elimination mechanism. One human T-cell donor supplies the culture work and selected human components of the mouse model. All functional experiments use lot A; lots B and C have identity data only. The matched cellular comparator uses the same carrier, CAR-X and total RNA without R, with D-present, D-absent and D-alone controls only where specified.

In the fictional packet’s mixed-cell culture at 24 hours, 1,000 sampled viable cells include 100 T cells. RNA is detected in 60 T cells and 240 other cells; surface CAR in 50 T cells and 150 others; 40 T cells express both CAR and R. Unexposed controls are negative. CAR-positive T cells are 50/100, or 50 per cent of T cells, but T cells are 50/200, or 25 per cent of all CAR-positive cells. CAR-positive cells are 200/1,000, or 20 per cent of the whole sample; dual-positive T cells are 40/100, or 40 per cent of T cells. RNA, surface protein and coexpression are different readouts, and none measures killing or body-wide distribution.

In a second fictional card, wells start with 100 target cells. At 48 hours, mean killing is 80 per cent for P with D, 55 per cent for P without D and 50 per cent for the matched CAR-X cells lacking R with or without D. Antigen-X-knockout targets and unengineered T cells with D give five per cent. The matched comparisons support an R/D-associated contribution in this donor’s assay, while the knockout and D controls test alternatives. Three wells are technical replicates from one donor, not three donors; no uncertainty interval is supplied. Tumour entry, general benefit and human safety remain different questions.

The fictional healthy-epithelial-organoid card measures survival at 48 hours with D in both arms: 90 per cent with P-generated T cells and 95 per cent with matched CAR-X cells lacking R. There are two organoid donors and one T-cell donor. The five-percentage-point difference needs uncertainty and an interpretation of harm; no acceptable threshold is supplied. It neither tests every healthy tissue nor defines a clinical safety window. Expression, binding, cell injury in culture and organ injury in people are different observations.

The fictional mouse card compares administered carrier P with empty carrier, with D in both arms and six mice per arm. One selected day-seven blood sample has 120 dual-positive cells among 200 T cells, or 60 per cent; this is not the six-mouse denominator, and two treated biopsies contain few engineered cells. Mean tumour volume is stated as 100 cubic millimetres at baseline, then 300 for P and 1,000 for control at day 28. P is 70 per cent smaller than control but three times the stated baseline: reduced growth, not regression below baseline or cure. Later follow-up, spread and causes of poor entry are missing. Without a matched CAR-X-without-R mouse arm, the comparison cannot isolate R’s contribution or establish every animal’s outcome.

Matching the fictional payload identities of lots A, B and C does not transfer lot A’s functional results to B and C. These are three lots, not three independent cell donors; potency and post-storage performance need relevant measurements. Likewise, at 24 hours after D withdrawal the fictional support signal falls from 100 to 20 relative units versus 100 with continued D, an 80 per cent signal reduction, while 90 of 100 tracked cells remain. Those are three technical wells from the same donor. The result does not demonstrate cell elimination, absent CAR recognition or reversal of injury.

The fictional packet contains no human study, so it has no clinical response or adverse-event denominator. An absent dataset is not a zero-per-cent rate, and target cells killed in culture are not people with a study-defined objective response. For each card, state the claim earned, the claim not earned and the next measurement, carrying product, specimen, comparator, donor or participant denominator, time and uncertainty. Do not fill one product’s missing evidence with another’s success. On a logarithmic axis, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 are tenfold steps rather than equal additive changes. Early human activity, comparative benefit and transfer to another product remain distinct evidence levels.

Tuerxunyiming’s 2026 work provides another model-specific example. An engineered Sindbis-envelope lentiviral system delivered a CD19 CAR in NPG mice carrying human blood mononuclear cells and Raji lymphoma. The experiment compared repeated vector administration with infusion of cells engineered in culture, using selected mice with measured human T-cell engraftment. Tumour control and CAR-positive blood fractions were different readouts; the in vivo-generated group had a lower CAR-positive fraction than the infused-cell group. These are human-cell/mouse experiments, not treatment of people or proof of exclusive delivery in every tissue.

Frank’s 2020 humanised-mouse experiment used the CD3-targeted TR66.opt lentiviral vector carrying a CD19 CAR. Figure 7 compares vector alone, vector after IL-7 pretreatment and an IL-7 control, with five or six mice per group. Its blood readout separates the human CD3-positive, CD45-positive T-cell gate from CD3-negative, CD45-positive non-T cells and CD45-negative mouse cells. Enrichment in sampled T cells is not a whole-body exclusivity test. Blood CAR expression peaked around three to four weeks and declined toward baseline after five weeks. Each animal’s CD19-positive blood-cell level was expressed relative to its own day-zero value. B-cell loss lasted longer in the IL-7-pretreated group; B cells reappeared at six weeks with vector alone. Delivery, subsequent cell expansion, receptor detection and B-cell depletion are different measurements, so their time courses need not match.
records.principle: Deliver encoding instructions into a defined cell population in the body, then measure which cells are engineered, where they go, how long expression lasts and what those cells do.
strengths: Investigates an alternative to administering cells engineered outside the body
May reduce some separate ex vivo manufacturing steps in a specified process
limitations: Cell targeting, off-target engineering and immune responses require measurement
Instruction dose does not specify final cell number or functional exposure
Conditioning, repeat dosing and cost are product- and protocol-specific

records.name: Autologous CAR-T manufacturing, batch by batch
records.tldr: An autologous CAR T-cell product is made from the intended recipient's cells. Collection, engineering, culture, quality assessment and treatment scheduling are distinct steps.
records.summary: A defined ex vivo process receives starting material, selects or enriches cells as needed, activates and engineers them, cultures them under controlled conditions, and prepares material for testing, storage and administration. The sequence, vector or other gene-transfer method, culture duration, fresh or frozen handling and assays depend on the product. A collection, manufacturing run, product lot, test sample and administered dose are not interchangeable units. One collection can yield multiple containers or doses; a run need not culminate in an infused treatment.

21 CFR Part 1271: human cells, tissues and cellular products
Wikipedia
FDA: CAR T-cell development guidance, January 2024

notes: Enrichment changes the composition of a mixture; activation changes cell state; expansion increases the absolute number of a defined living population. Measure the intended population consistently before and after culture. A higher percentage, a different volume or a higher concentration alone does not demonstrate expansion.

Release evidence retains identity, purity, viable amount, intended biological activity and relevant contamination risks. Some tests can continue after disposition only within a justified and authorised setting with appropriate follow-up. Neither receptor expression nor a viable-cell count alone establishes every required function.

Culture duration is only one clock. Collection-to-infusion also includes material acceptance, transport, processing, testing, clinical reassessment and scheduling, with steps sometimes overlapping. A number measured among infused recipients does not describe people who never reached infusion. Avoid a universal week range or a cross-product timing ranking.

Manufacturing can end without a product, yield a product outside specified requirements, or provide a conforming lot that is never administered. A lack of a collection or treatment slot is another access event. Keep the report's event definition, denominator, period and cancellation rules with any rate.

The process remains traceable through collections, intermediate material, product lots, doses and samples. Source and intended-recipient matching, biological identity testing, custody and conditions, lot disposition and clinical readiness each require their own evidence.

FDA's 2024 document focuses on ex vivo CAR T-cell development. Its recommendations do not automatically validate every in vivo carrier, other immune-cell product or research-bank process. Process changes need relevant evidence rather than a promise that automation or shorter culture preserves all attributes.

In a separate fictional cohort, ten people undergo collection and eight receive an infusion. The two never infused are reported separately; they are not assigned the collection-to-infusion time calculated among the eight. State the follow-up window and reasons for non-infusion before interpreting this proportion.
records.principle: Retain the product-specific process, starting material, defined cell population, parent/lot/dose relationships, control strategy and separate manufacturing and clinical outcomes.
strengths: Supports a defined recipient-linked manufacturing and quality-control process
Individual steps can be studied and improved with relevant comparability and functional evidence
limitations: Starting-material variability, contamination, growth or engineering problems can prevent a suitable product
A completed lot, a conforming lot, shipment and infusion are distinct outcomes
Shorter culture does not establish a shorter total wait, equivalent quality or better clinical outcomes

records.name: Companion diagnostics
records.tldr: A companion diagnostic supplies information needed for a corresponding medicine to be used safely and effectively. Its labeling defines the intended use of the result.
records.summary: FDA describes companion diagnostics as devices that supply essential information for a corresponding treatment. Their roles can include identifying likely benefit, increased risk of serious adverse effects or a specified monitoring need. The treatment label and diagnostic labeling retain the relevant disease, specimen, biomarker and decision rule. Some devices have documented group labeling for specified oncology therapies. Similar analyte names do not establish assay interchangeability, and a label-matched result does not guarantee individual benefit or complete clinical suitability.

records.name: Accelerated approval
records.tldr: This FDA pathway can authorize a specified use based on an endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. Further studies must confirm the anticipated benefit.
records.summary: Accelerated approval is a marketing approval for an indication, distinct from a development designation. FDA can use a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict benefit for an eligible serious condition. Required studies must confirm the anticipated benefit; the use can receive traditional approval or undergo withdrawal through the applicable process. A preliminary laboratory signal, a product name or a historical announcement does not establish current approval for a particular use.

records.summary: Fast Track supports development and review for drugs addressing serious conditions and unmet need. Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation has its own eligible-product and preliminary-clinical-evidence criteria. Breakthrough Therapy and Priority Review likewise have distinct purposes; review support is not an efficacy result or a guarantee of approval or delivery timing. Accelerated approval, in contrast, is an approval pathway with benefit-confirmation requirements. Read the named program and the actual product decision separately.

records.name: FDA laboratory-developed test (LDT) rule
records.tldr: A laboratory-developed test is described by its development and use within a laboratory. Laboratory oversight, product authorization and evidence supporting a particular test use are separate questions.
records.summary: FDA issued its laboratory-developed-test rule in May 2024. Its current notice states that a federal court vacated that rule in March 2025 and that FDA restored the earlier regulatory text in September 2025. The vacated phaseout schedule should not be presented as a current requirement. An LDT description alone does not establish FDA authorization, research-only status or clinical usefulness. Check the actual laboratory, product and intended use rather than assigning every LDT one approval or evidence status.

records.tldr: Laboratory certification addresses the laboratory and its testing quality. Product authorization and evidence that a particular test use helps patients answer separate questions.

CMS distinguishes analytical oversight under that program from clinical validity, which concerns what a result means for a clinical condition. A research-use label describes intended purpose; a laboratory-developed-test description concerns how and where a test is developed and used. FDA product authorization concerns a specified product and intended use. These descriptions can coexist and do not form one universal ladder of clinical usefulness or payment.

An entry in FDA establishment registration or device listing does not itself mean that the facility or device is approved, cleared or authorized. Registration and product authorization are separate claims.

Three examples separate intended uses. Validated ER immunohistochemistry in invasive breast cancer, with appropriate tissue handling, tumour-nucleus scoring and controls, has a marker-specific pathology and endocrine-treatment assessment role; it does not validate a new RNA score as a substitute. In a wholly fictional second example, assay T version 1 detects alteration M in fixed tumour tissue under rule R, and Drug A requires exactly that result in setting S. The stipulated match supplies that requirement within the exercise, without promising benefit; another specimen, result type or setting needs evidence for the changed use. A third fictional score Q combines RNA, spatial neighbourhoods and a derived culture response to propose Drug A. Reproducibility and biological support can justify research, but do not establish that Q-guided care improves outcomes against an appropriate comparator. A laboratory certificate does not supply that missing evidence. Useful research and an established clinical use can appear on different parts of one report.

records.name: Expanded access (compassionate use)
records.tldr: Expanded access permits qualifying treatment use of an investigational drug outside a clinical trial. Supply, physician responsibility and applicable regulatory and ethics requirements still need to be met.
records.summary: United States, federal regulation: drug and biologic expanded access has individual-patient, intermediate-population and widespread-treatment arrangements. Criteria include serious or immediately life-threatening illness, no comparable satisfactory alternative, justified potential benefit and risk, and no interference with clinical development. A new individual-patient IND is different from a protocol under an existing active IND. Supplier agreement and applicable FDA, ethics-review and consent requirements remain separate from manufacture, institutional readiness and scheduling. Access authorization is not evidence that treatment improves outcomes.

notes: For non-emergency individual-patient use, a new IND ordinarily becomes effective 30 calendar days after FDA receipt unless held or FDA permits earlier use. An individual-patient protocol under an existing active IND has no automatic 30-day wait, but must be submitted and have applicable IRB approval and consent. Widespread-use treatment protocols have different start rules.

Emergency individual-patient use can receive prior FDA authorisation by telephone or other rapid communication, allowing use to begin before the written expanded-access submission. That submission is due within 15 working days of FDA authorisation. When there is insufficient time for prospective institutional review board (IRB) review, report the emergency use to the IRB within 5 working days of starting treatment. Subsequent use at the same institution normally requires prior IRB review. FDA's April 2026 guidance also describes discretion for a subsequent emergency request when prior review is infeasible, with the same 5-working-day reporting requirement. This is not continuing permission or a promised treatment date.

A licensed physician acting as sponsor-investigator can use Form FDA 3926 for an individual-patient expanded-access IND in a non-emergency or emergency setting. Forms FDA 1571 and 1572 remain an alternative. FDA also lists eRequest for non-emergency individual-patient requests. The streamlined form is not a marketing application, a form for group requests or the device-access process.

When an application references another sponsor’s IND, a letter of authorization permits FDA to reference specified product information. That permission does not itself authorize treatment or guarantee drug supply. If such a letter is unavailable, the FDA review division can advise which other information may satisfy the applicable requirements.

For an unapproved investigational drug supplied under an IND, the IND sponsor needs separate prior written FDA authorization to charge for the drug. Recoverable costs and other conditions differ between clinical trials and expanded access. Treatment authorization does not itself authorize charging, and permission to recover drug costs does not decide insurer payment or the total cost of clinical care.

A reported FDA authorization rate needs its stated submitted-request denominator, period and request categories. It does not measure the fraction of everyone seeking the drug who obtains manufacturer supply, meets every requirement or actually receives treatment. An application authorization is not a personal probability of access or benefit.

For individual-patient expanded access, authorised drug-cost recovery is limited to direct costs attributable specifically to supplying the drug for that authorised investigational use. Examples include per-unit manufacture or acquisition, shipping and storage. Commercial-scale facilities and equipment, and research, administrative or labour expenses that would occur anyway, are indirect costs excluded by 21 CFR 312.8(d)(1). This concerns the sponsor's authorised drug charge, not every bill for clinical care.

For intermediate-size populations and treatment INDs or protocols under 21 CFR 312.315 and 312.320, the regulation additionally permits specified monitoring, IND reporting and directly associated administrative costs. Those additional categories do not apply automatically to an individual-patient arrangement. FDA authorisation of the treatment and prior written permission to charge remain separate.

FDA's request-forms page reports that, on average, 99% of expanded-access requests may proceed. That is the page's submitted-request statement, without a period specified there, not the fraction of everyone seeking a drug who receives it or benefits. Manufacturer agreement is an independent supply gate, and Project Facilitate is an FDA oncology point of contact that helps clinicians navigate requests. The reported FDA fraction does not measure how often supply is the limiting step or rank the obstacles in a particular plan.

The charging calculation required by 21 CFR 312.8(d)(3) must have supporting documentation and a statement that an independent certified public accountant reviewed and approved it. Expanded-access permission to charge normally lasts one year from FDA authorisation, or less if FDA specifies; the sponsor can request reauthorisation. FDA must withdraw permission if charging interferes with development or its authorisation criteria cease to be met. A two-year-old letter therefore needs a current reauthorisation check. These rules concern the investigational drug charge, not a promise of free clinical care.

Build a readiness record around the actual product, formulation, dose, route and schedule, its clinical rationale and alternatives, and the supporting quality, exposure and safety information. Name the sponsor and treating clinician, supplier and receiving or storage team, administering service, urgent-care destination, and people responsible for response assessment, toxicity management and reporting. Record the applicable submissions, review and consent, usable supply, costs, dependencies and possible stop conditions. Mark each answer confirmed, proposed or unknown with its responsible person and date; a checklist does not determine a patient's status. The treating team must assess suitability before administration; a laboratory result supplies neither eligibility nor a safe regimen. This checklist concerns U.S. drugs and biologics; device access, other countries and institutional rules can differ.

In a fictional request, a supplier says manufacture could finish next week while institutional review, the treatment plan and monitoring remain unresolved. That is a manufacturing estimate, not a treatment date. Similarly, FDA permission without a service able to administer and monitor the product leaves a delivery gate open. Ask which milestones are complete and which depend on others. A fictional new non-emergency individual-patient IND with supplier agreement, the necessary product information, applicable IRB review and consent can proceed when effective, ordinarily 30 days after FDA receipt or earlier FDA notice, provided it is not on hold. Supplier review, manufacture, FDA review, institutional review, shipping and scheduling each need their own estimate and dependencies.

For non-emergency individual-patient use, a physician using Form FDA 3926 may request the permitted institutional review board (IRB) chairperson or designated-member concurrence procedure instead of review at a convened full-board meeting. Concurrence must precede treatment under that procedure. It is not a waiver of informed consent: obtain the applicable written consent on an IRB-approved form. The supplier's letter of authorisation lets FDA reference specified information and does not replace these steps or FDA permission to proceed.

records.name: CAR-T cell therapy
records.tldr: CAR-T therapy uses T cells carrying an engineered receptor. Approved products treat selected blood cancers, with product-specific eligibility and safety requirements.
records.summary:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

notes: Generation labels describe common signaling architectures. First-generation constructs use an activation domain, often CD3 zeta; second-generation designs add one costimulatory region; third-generation designs combine two. Fourth-generation and later labels vary across authors. More domains do not establish better patient outcomes. The full binder, spacer, anchor, signaling arrangement and cell preparation still matter.

CD28 and 4-1BB are borrowed intracellular signaling regions, not separately administered receptors. Kawalekar compared metabolic and memory features in defined human-cell experiments. Ramos co-infused two specified second- and third-generation products in lymphoma; different expansion and persistence did not isolate comparative clinical benefit. Neither study ranks all products by signaling-domain name.

Binding, surface CAR expression, activation, proliferation and completed target-cell killing are distinct readouts. Compare otherwise matched constructs, target-positive and target-negative cells, healthy-tissue targets and unstimulated activity. Hudecek found that particular IgG-derived spacers could support killing in a dish yet impair activity in mouse models through Fc interactions.

A peptide-HLA target is an exception to blanket HLA-independent descriptions. Rafiq tested a WT1 peptide presented by HLA-A*02:01 in cell and mouse models; this was a proof of concept, not evidence that every intracellular protein or every HLA type is addressable by that construct.

A 2024 preprint used a pooled signaling-domain library, repeated stimulation and single-cell sequencing to study how domain arrangement affected T-cell states over time. Its membrane-proximal-domain findings are construct-and-assay observations, not a clinical ranking of domains or a validation of pooled-screen hits as treatments.

FDA initiated boxed-warning changes in 2024 for the risk of T-cell malignancies after the then-approved BCMA- or CD19-directed autologous CAR T-cell products. Its communication calls for lifelong monitoring for secondary malignancies. This is a scoped regulatory warning, not a claim that every type of engineered immune cell has the same risk.

In June 2025, FDA eliminated REMS requirements for the named autologous CAR T-cell products in its notice. Product warnings and safety monitoring continued. The manufacturer postmarketing observational studies with 15-year follow-up described in that notice are different from the lifelong patient-monitoring statement in the earlier safety communication.

A receptor-bearing cell, its genetic instructions and its receptor protein are different objects. For a protein-coding instruction, DNA is transcribed into RNA, and a ribosome translates usable messenger RNA into protein. Delivered messenger RNA starts at the translation step. Folding and transport to the membrane still have to occur before a surface receptor can bind its target. In this schematic sequence, simplified shapes and an arrow from recognition toward a response do not show that every cell expressed the receptor or completed killing.

Kymriah’s product description illustrates why borrowed parts do not identify the whole product. Its CD19-binding region is a murine-derived single-chain antibody fragment, followed by a CD8-derived hinge and transmembrane region and the internal 4-1BB/CD137 and CD3-zeta signalling domains. CD8 here names the origin of structural segments, not a claim that the infused preparation contains only CD8 T cells. The label describes enrichment for T cells and permits other cell populations. Autologous source, domain names and architecture do not transfer Kymriah’s clinical results to another construct.

Suppose two fictional CARs differ only in their hinge: both bind purified antigen, but only one kills antigen-bearing cells. Compare surface expression and the geometry of cell contact before concluding that affinity is the problem. Likewise, DNA-positive cells without killing leave RNA production, receptor folding and trafficking, actual binding and signalling as separate possible failure points. Hudecek’s R11 ROR1 experiments illustrate a product-specific constraint: a long spacer enabled recognition of its membrane-proximal epitope, while changes that reduced Fc-receptor binding improved activity in the tested mice. Longer is not a universal design rule. Treat the transmembrane segment as part of the finished construct: assess assembly, surface expression and interactions rather than presume it is a neutral anchor. Unstimulated signalling and responses to repeated target encounters also need separate assessment.

In a fictional population of 100 cancer cells, 80 display target X and 20 do not. Killing the X-positive 80 leaves 20 survivors; ten times as many effector cells does not create X on them. For two targets, suppose 20 cells carry both X and Y, 60 carry X only, ten Y only and ten neither. An idealised either-target rule covers 90 cells, whereas a both-target rule covers 20. These are recognition-coverage calculations, not measured killing or healthy-tissue selectivity. Expression thresholds, tissue access and cell function still matter.

TNBC describes a breast-cancer subtype, not one universal receptor target. A research programme, a positive stain or a named cell platform does not establish a treatment indication or rank safe recognition strategies. The cited TROP2 work supplies preclinical observations, and the ROR1 phase-I report supplies limited activity and infiltration observations in its actual mixed population. These studies do not supply a comparative clinical-benefit estimate for every antigen-directed product in TNBC. Individual labels and clinical studies define their own disease, regimen and eligibility scope.

Kawalekar’s defined human-CAR experiments linked 4-1BB signalling to outgrowth of CD8 central-memory cells with greater respiratory capacity, fatty-acid oxidation and mitochondrial biogenesis. CD28-containing CARs produced effector-memory cells with a gene-expression pattern consistent with greater glycolysis. These are construct-and-system observations, not a ranking of clinical speed, persistence or safety by domain name. Other receptor parts, preparation, starting-cell state, target and disease setting remain relevant. Ramos simultaneously infused separately tracked second- and third-generation products. Their different expansion and persistence did not let a shared tumour response isolate either product’s clinical contribution.

Relapse mechanisms need separate investigation. Sotillo found CD19 sequence and splicing changes affecting recognition in B-ALL relapse material and experiments. Deng found infusion-product transcriptional features associated with outcomes in a selected cohort of 24 large B-cell lymphoma infusion products; those associations did not prove that one engineered modification would correct every failure.
records.principle: A common CAR presents a binder outside the cell and signaling domains inside it, connected through a spacer and transmembrane region. Conventional surface-antigen recognition can bypass peptide-HLA presentation; specialized peptide-HLA-targeting CARs retain the relevant HLA and antigen-processing requirements.
strengths: Antigen-directed recognition in engineered T cells
Established uses for specific products in selected blood cancers
limitations: Shared healthy-tissue targets and inflammatory, neurologic or blood-count harms
Manufacturing, access and cost depend on the product and setting
Antigen heterogeneity, cell state, tissue access and local inhibition

records.name: AAV (adeno-associated virus) vector
records.tldr: An AAV vector is a small engineered virus particle used to carry a DNA cassette into cells. Reaching a cell, keeping the DNA and making useful protein are separate steps, and each needs its own evidence in the cells that matter.
records.summary:
Recombinant AAV replaces the viral coding sequence with a designed cassette and regulatory sequences. The protein shell (capsid) influences which cells the particle enters; the cassette decides what those cells could make. The DNA still has to reach the nucleus and act as a template before RNA and protein appear, and an AAV is a different virus from an adenovirus.

Where the DNA sits was measured in different systems. In sequential muscle biopsies taken 3 and 12 months after an intramuscular AAV vector expressing alpha-1 antitrypsin, most vector DNA was double-stranded circular episomes, and clones recovered from the biopsies were transcriptionally active (Schnepp and colleagues; abstract read, full text not retrievable). After partial hepatectomy in mice, extrachromosomal genomes were the main form behind liver expression and in most cases no more than about 10 per cent of stably transduced genomes had integrated, although one of three mice at a higher dose had 67 per cent integrated genomes (Nakai and colleagues). That shows the usual behaviour of the tested vectors in those tissues, not that integration never happens, and persistent DNA does not show an intact cassette, enough protein or a surviving functional cell: in the muscle study the episomal inverted terminal repeats ranged from fully intact to severely deleted, so counting vector DNA is a different measurement from showing a working cassette.

Immunity and capacity also limit what a lot can do. In a phase 1/2 study in seven people with severe haemophilia B, an AAV2 factor IX vector infused through the hepatic artery reached therapeutic levels at the highest dose but expression lasted about 8 weeks; the authors' further studies suggested that cell-mediated immunity against capsid antigens destroyed transduced hepatocytes (Manno and colleagues). Neutralising antibodies against the capsid are why re-dosing is hard: a review notes that systemic AAV dosing needs patient stratification by antibody level and that re-administration then becomes very difficult (Naso and colleagues), and a 2024 mouse study, which opens by noting that AAV typically induces long-lasting neutralising antibodies that prevent re-administration, found that transient B-cell depletion (anti-CD20 with anti-BAFF) before hepatic AAV8 delivery allowed effective re-administration (Rana and colleagues). Whether a given product can be given again is a product-specific question, and that mouse experiment does not establish a clinical re-dosing protocol. For packaging, the AAV2 genome is a single-stranded DNA of 4,675 nucleotides (Srivastava and colleagues) and the original self-complementary-vector experiment used an inverted repeat that could pair with itself, bypassing synthesis of the second strand (McCarty and colleagues, 2001). McCarty's later review describes the trade-off as losing half the coding capacity. Report the capsid, cassette configuration and length being measured with a capacity figure; a measured packaged-genome length and usable coding capacity answer different questions. In the study of plasmid-encoded vectors of 4.7 to 8.7 kb in AAV2, AAV5 and AAV8 capsids, packaged genomes never exceeded 5.2 kb; genomes from plasmids over 5 kb were heterogeneous and truncated at the 5' end, and reporter expression in cells at high multiplicity of infection was substantially lower than from genomes under 5 kb (Wu and colleagues). FDA follow-up guidance says vectors such as AAV that do not tend to integrate or reactivate generally carry a lower risk of delayed adverse events, while product-specific modifications may change that, so safety is assessed per product.

AAV also appears in cell-engineering workflows without being the lasting product. In primary human T cells in culture, Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA were electroporated and a recombinant AAV6 vector added 2 to 4 hours later supplied a repair template encoding a CD19 CAR, which was knocked into the TRAC locus; the edited cells outperformed conventionally generated CAR T cells in a mouse leukaemia model (Eyquem and colleagues). There the AAV carried a donor template into cells outside the body and the lasting change was the knocked-in receptor, so an AAV in a workflow does not show direct targeting of T cells in a patient. Capsid variants differ in tissue tropism, for example AAV8 for liver in rodents and non-human primates (Naso and colleagues).

Muscle and liver observations, T-cell editing in culture and mouse leukaemia experiments answer different questions. Muscle or liver persistence does not establish how another cassette behaves in dividing T cells. A capsid that favours a tissue is a delivery feature, separate from what the encoded protein recognises; the cited experiments do not establish benefit for people with cancer.

notes: Measure vector DNA with its cell or tissue denominator and distinguish genome integrity, DNA form, RNA, protein and function. An average DNA count does not identify an episome or an insertion site. A long-lived signal in one tissue does not establish survival, expression or genetic inheritance in a different dividing-cell population. Nonintegrated genomes can be diluted as cells divide. In Nakai's mouse liver-regeneration experiment, vector genomes per cell and factor IX expression fell after partial hepatectomy, whereas the integrated transposon comparator retained expression; this is a defined tissue/regeneration comparison.

records.name: Targeted lipid nanoparticles
records.tldr: Targeted lipid nanoparticles use a surface ligand or a changed lipid mix to favour particular cells or organs. Enrichment in a tissue is not the same as working protein made only in the intended cell type.
records.summary:
Two strategies are separate. A ligand strategy adds a binding molecule such as an antibody to the particle surface so it recognises a marker on intended cells; binding must still lead to uptake and usable release, and the marker may sit on other cells. A formulation strategy changes the lipids: selective organ targeting (SORT) added a supplemental lipid to otherwise standard LNPs and, after intravenous injection in mice, shifted delivery toward lung, spleen or liver; with a Cre reporter, the lung formulation edited about 40 per cent of epithelial and 65 per cent of endothelial cells, the spleen formulation 12 per cent of B cells and 10 per cent of T cells, and the liver formulation 93 per cent of hepatocytes (Cheng and colleagues, as reported). These are measured results in mice, not a rule connecting a composition to an organ in people.

A CD5-directed example shows both the aim and its limit. CD5-targeted LNPs carrying modified mRNA for a chimeric antigen receptor against fibroblast activation protein were tested in activated mouse T cells in culture (81 per cent expressed a GFP reporter and 83 per cent the receptor, against 7 per cent with isotype-control antibody particles) and then injected intravenously into mice with angiotensin II and phenylephrine induced cardiac injury. Receptor expression appeared in each major T-cell subset by flow cytometry (87 per cent of receptor-positive T cells were CD4-positive), bioluminescence showed spleen targeting only with CD5 particles, and liver expression occurred with both CD5 and control particles, so an organ-level signal and the identity of the expressing cells were measured separately; treatment reduced fibrosis and restored cardiac function in these mice (Rurik and colleagues, author manuscript). The delivery address was CD5 and the encoded receptor recognised a different target. This was a fibrosis model, not a cancer trial, and the authors disclose patents on the platforms.

A later study used targeted LNPs to deliver mRNA to specific T-cell subsets; its abstract reports reprogrammed CD8-positive T cells in samples from healthy donors and people with autoimmune disease, tumour control in humanised mice and B-cell depletion in cynomolgus monkeys (Hunter and colleagues; abstract only, full text not retrievable). Each of those is a different experiment in a different setting, and none is evidence of benefit against solid tumours in people.

Enrichment is not exclusivity. In a Cre-reporter experiment recombination appeared in 81.1 per cent of CD4-positive and 75.6 per cent of CD8-positive splenocytes but also in 15.0 per cent of CD3-negative cells, mainly B cells, dendritic cells and macrophages (Rurik and colleagues), and the 87 per cent figure above is a share of receptor-positive cells, not the share of CD4 T cells that expressed the receptor, so the denominator matters. Cargo type also matters for how long the effect lasts: RNA encoding a receptor produced transient CAR T cells in that study, whereas RNA encoding a genome editor can leave a lasting DNA change, as when SORT lipid nanoparticles delivered Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA to edit cells in mice (Cheng and colleagues) and Cas9 mRNA with an AAV repair template knocked a CAR into T cells in culture (Eyquem and colleagues).

Organ signal, cell identity, protein function and clinical effect need separate measurements, with matched untargeted controls and identified intended and unintended recipient populations.
